ta-l1d5q2-d1e100.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the second inquiry of Distinction 5: whether the essence is related to generation as that from which (de quo) it occurs. Two articles follow: whether the Son is begotten from the Father's substance, and whether he is from nothing.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e112.summary: First objection that the Son is not begotten from the Father's substance. Every preposition is transitive, and transition requires diversity or distinction. The Son is not distinct from the Father's essence, so he cannot be said to be born from it.
claims: Prepositions imply transition, which requires distinction.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e115.summary: Second objection. Human nature relates to Socrates as the divine essence to the Son, and Socrates is not said to be 'from human essence'. So neither is the Son 'from the Father's essence'.
claims: Individuals are not said to be from their nature.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e118.summary: Third objection. 'From' (de) always implies order, but between the Son and the essence there is no order of time, of nature (since the essence does not beget), or of causality.
claims: 'De' implies order, and there is no order between Son and essence.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e122.summary: Anticipates the reply that the phrase expresses the Son's consubstantiality with the Father. The Father's essence is the Son's, and the Son's whole essence is in the Father, so by that reasoning one could equally say the Father is from the Son's substance.
claims: Consubstantiality is symmetric between Father and Son.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e125.summary: Notes that the contrary is shown by authorities in Lombard's text.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e128.summary: Thomas's determination. The preposition 'de' properly designates both principle and consubstantiality, while 'ex' designates only order of principle. Whatever is 'de' something is 'ex' it, but not conversely (cf. Dist. 36). 'Ex' can mark temporal order (day from morning), agent principle (artifacts from the artisan), or material principle (a knife from iron). 'De', implying consubstantiality, always marks either a material principle (a knife of iron) or a consubstantial agent (a son begotten of his father by a division of substance). In this way the Son is 'of' the Father, as begetter, and 'of' the Father's essence, as the communicated principle of generation. This approaches a material likeness once every imperfection of matter is removed and only this condition remains: that it stays in the thing and the thing subsists through it.
claims: 'De' signifies principle with consubstantiality; 'ex' signifies only order of principle.
The Son is 'of' the Father as begetter and 'of' his essence as the communicated principle of generation.
The essence functions like matter only in remaining in the Son and making him subsist.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e131.summary: Reply to the first objection. 'De' implies consubstantiality and order to a principle. Consubstantiality concerns the essence, and order, which is the ground of transition, concerns the begetting person. We do not say the Son is 'of the essence' but 'of the essence of the Father', so the Son need be distinct from the Father, not from the essence.
claims: In 'de essentia patris' the transitive order refers to the Father, the consubstantiality to the essence.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the second objection. Socrates too is born 'of' his father's nature or substance, but differently: the Son of God is of the Father's whole substance, Socrates of part of it. Socrates also subsists not only through essence but through matter, which individuates his human nature, whereas the Son subsists through the Father's essence, which is not part of the Son but the whole that the Son is.
claims: The Son is of the Father's whole substance; a human son is of part of his father's substance.
The Son subsists through the Father's essence as the whole of what he is.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e137.summary: The third objection is answered as the first was.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. The phrase signifies not only consubstantiality but also order to a principle, which would not be kept if one said the Father is of the Son's essence.
claims: 'De essentia' implies order of origin as well as consubstantiality, so it is not symmetric.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e153.summary: First objection that the Son is from nothing. What is not from pre-existing matter is said to be from nothing, and the Son is not from anything as from matter.
claims: What is not from pre-existing matter is from nothing.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e156.summary: Second objection. Whatever has being only from another is non-being in itself, since there is no mean between being and non-being. The Son has being only from the Father, so of himself he has non-being, and everything of that kind is from nothing (Avicenna).
claims: What has being only from another is of itself non-being and so from nothing.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e159.summary: Sed contra. Whatever is from nothing is created, and the Son is uncreated.
claims: Whatever is from nothing is created.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e163.summary: Second sed contra from Damascene: whatever is from nothing can turn into nothing, and the Son cannot.
claims: What is from nothing is capable of returning to nothing.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e166.summary: Thomas's determination. Saying that something is not from anything differs from saying that it is from nothing. The first posits nothing and is true of the Son, who is not from matter. The second affirms an order to nothing, which can be temporal or natural. Temporal order means first not being and then being, which fits nothing eternal. Natural order holds when something has dependent being: of itself it has only non-being, since its whole being depends on another, and what a thing has of itself naturally precedes what it has from another. So even if the heavens were eternal, they would still be from nothing (Avicenna). The Son has neither order to nothing. He is eternal, and his being is absolute, not dependent on another.
claims: Not being from anything differs from being from nothing.
Being from nothing implies an order to nothing, temporal or natural; even an eternal creature would be from nothing by natural order.
The Son has no order to nothing, since he is eternal and his being is not dependent.
concepts: order of time vs. order of nature

ta-l1d5q2-d1e169.summary: Reply to the first objection. Although the Son is not from matter, it does not follow that he is not from anything, since he is from the Father's substance. Even setting that aside, it would not follow that he is from nothing: the Father is not from anything yet not from nothing, and Father and Son have the same being.
claims: The Son is from the Father's substance; and even what is from nothing material need not be from nothing.

ta-l1d5q2-d1e172.summary: Reply to the second objection. Although the Son has his whole being from another, his being is not dependent, because he receives from the Father numerically the same being the Father has. So his being is not dependent, not merely possible, and not from nothing, which would follow if he received a numerically other being.
claims: The Son receives numerically the same being as the Father, so his being is not dependent or possible.

ta-l1d5q2-Dd1e95.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 asks whether the essence is that from which the Son is generated, in two articles: whether the Son is from the Father's substance and whether he is from nothing.

ta-l1d5q2-Dd1e104.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Son is begotten from the Father's substance. Objections argue from the transitivity of prepositions, the analogy with Socrates and human nature, the lack of order between Son and essence, and the symmetry of consubstantiality. Thomas distinguishes 'de', which implies principle with consubstantiality, from 'ex', which implies only order. The Son is 'of' the Father as begetter and 'of' the Father's essence as the communicated principle, which plays a matter-like role purified of imperfection. The replies refer the transitive order to the Father and the consubstantiality to the essence. They contrast the whole-substance divine generation with partial human generation, and they note the asymmetry of order between Father and Son.
claims: The Son is truly begotten 'de substantia patris'.
'De' signifies consubstantial principle, 'ex' only order of principle.

ta-l1d5q2-Dd1e145.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Son is from nothing. Objections argue that he is not from matter and that whatever has being from another is of itself non-being (Avicenna). The sed contra arguments note that whatever is from nothing is created and can lapse into nothing. Thomas distinguishes 'not from anything' from 'from nothing', which implies an order to nothing, either temporal or natural (dependent being). Even an eternal creature would be from nothing by natural order. The Son is neither, because he is eternal and receives numerically the same independent being as the Father.
claims: The Son is not from nothing, since he has neither temporal nor natural order to non-being.
Even an eternal creature would be from nothing by natural order of dependence.

ta-l1d5q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 5 asks whether the divine essence is that from which the Son is generated. Article 1 holds that the Son is begotten 'of the substance of the Father', distinguishing 'de' (consubstantial principle) from 'ex' (mere order). The Father is the begetter and his essence the communicated principle, which remains in the Son and makes him subsist, like matter purified of imperfection. Article 2 denies that the Son is from nothing. Being 'from nothing' implies an order to non-being, temporal or by dependence, and the eternal Son receives numerically the same, non-dependent being as the Father. Thomas notes, following Avicenna, that even an eternal creature would be from nothing by natural order.
claims: The Son is begotten from the Father's substance as from a consubstantial principle.
The Son is not from nothing, since he receives the Father's numerically identical, independent being.
An eternal creature would still be from nothing by natural dependence.
